cues.text: Jerome the Scholar

Born around 340 in Stridon on the Dalmatian frontier, Jerome studied in Rome, traveled through Gaul, and lived for years as a hermit in the Syrian desert, mastering Greek and, unusually for a Latin Christian of his day, Hebrew.
He returned to Rome around 382 already recognized as the Church's foremost living biblical scholar.
Commission from Pope Damasus
In Rome, Pope Damasus I commissioned Jerome to revise the confused and inconsistent Old Latin ( Vetus Latina ) versions of the Gospels then circulating.
Jerome's revised Gospel text appeared around 383.
What began as a papal commission to fix the Gospels grew, on Jerome's own initiative, into a far larger undertaking: a fresh translation of nearly the whole Bible.
Bethlehem and the Hebrew Truth
After Damasus died in 384, Jerome settled permanently at Bethlehem , establishing a monastery near the traditional site of Christ's birth.

There he undertook the boldest part of his work: translating the Old Testament not from the Greek Septuagint, as tradition favored, but directly from the Hebrew original, a method he defended as recovering the Hebraica veritas — the 'Hebrew truth.'
This approach drew sharp criticism, including from St. Augustine, who worried it would divide Latin churches using different Old Testaments.
Jerome pressed on regardless, completing his Hebrew-based Old Testament around 405, after more than two decades of labor alongside his New Testament revisions.
Controversies and Convictions
Jerome was famous for his fierce, uncompromising temperament as much as his scholarship, and his translation choices provoked real theological disputes over favored readings and renderings.
Yet his conviction about the necessity of Scripture study never wavered, expressed in his most quoted line, written in the prologue to his commentary on Isaiah.
Legacy: The Bible of the West
Jerome's translation, only gradually adopted, eventually eclipsed the older Latin versions and by the Middle Ages was known simply as the versio vulgata — the 'commonly used version,' or Vulgate .
It became the Scripture of Western monasticism, scholasticism, and preaching for over a thousand years.
The Vulgate at Trent and Beyond
The Council of Trent in the sixteenth century formally declared the Vulgate the Church's authentic Latin Scripture text for public reading, disputation, and preaching.
This prompted official revisions culminating in the Clementine edition of 1592, which remained standard until the Nova Vulgata of 1979.
